podcast.title: Band Name Origin
podcast.body: The band adopted their name from The Power Station studio in New York, a place they loved so much for its distinctive sound, particularly the drums. "They loved that place so much that they named their group after the studio."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Exemplar of 1980s Drum Sound
podcast.body: The band, featuring Robert Palmer, members of Duran Duran, and drummer Tony Thompson, is highlighted as a prime example of the pervasive drum sound of the 1980s. This sound was characterized by its big, boomy, and powerful quality, often achieved by recording in large, reverberant rooms and augmenting with electronic effects like gated reverbs. "The Power Station featuring Robert Palmer, a couple of guys from Durandoran and drummer Tony Thompson. That is an example of the drum sound that was very much invoked in the 1980s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Music Questions People Almost Never Ask

xref.title: Founding and Location (1977)
xref.body: The Power Station, located in New York at approximately 53rd and 10th, was founded in 1977 by Tony Bongiovi, the second cousin of John Bon Jovi. The building previously served as a Consolidated Edison power plant and later a TV studio for "Let's Make a Deal." "In 1977, the building was bought and rebuilt as a recording studio by Tony Bongeovi, the second cousin of some New Jersey kid named John Bongeovi."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Current Status (Avatar Studios)
xref.body: The Power Station continues to operate today under a new name, Avatar Studios. "The power station still exists, although it's not called that anymore."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Distinctive Drum Sound
xref.body: A key characteristic of recordings from The Power Station was its unique drum sound, described as "big, powerful and boomed." This was achieved through the studio's special ambient acoustics, sometimes augmented with noise gates on kits like Tony Thompson's. "The biggest difference between the power station and just about everywhere else was how drums sounded."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Forced Studio Change
xref.body: The Clash were compelled to leave The Power Station studio when their recording budget ran out, leading them to relocate their sessions to Electric Lady Studios. "The clash had been working at another studio called the Power Station, but the clash were kicked out when the money ran out."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influence on Rock Recording
xref.body: The Power Station's innovative acoustic approach gained immense popularity, profoundly changing rock recording techniques for years. It fostered a demand for bigger drum sounds, moving away from close-miking and instead leveraging natural room reverb found in large spaces. "The power station, the studio, their approach was so popular that it changed the way many rock recordings were made for years."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Innovative Reverberation Time-Based Design
xref.body: Bongiovi designed The Power Station as a "reverberation time-based studio," incorporating a deliberate, slight reverb of about three-quarters of a second in the main recording room. This decay time matched that of the original Motown Studios in Detroit, resulting in records that sounded "live in full of energy." "Tony Bongeovi built the power station as a reverberation time-based studio."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
